<reason>Both sides argued tightly and vividly, and CON's "even if" focus plus the swap-contradiction charge in [B4.4-4.5] and the "dispatch hears pacing, not the knife" point created real pressure. But PRO did more of the decisive comparative work: it turned CON's own scenes (pills, traffic, medical crash) into medic calls, isolated the knife scenario as the one where the armed responder authors the death, and by Rebuttal 2 had narrowed CON's unique speed benefit to a hypothetical sister-in-the-gap while placing a widely known, recurring mechanism (police killings of people in crisis) on the other side of the ledger. PRO also answered CON's cap question with a plausible, ordinary mechanism (dispatch priority tiers) and flipped the "unbounded" charge onto CON's undated training reform ("trainable vs trained"). CON's best late line—shooting happens after arrival, the wait before—distinguishes the two harms but never engages the frequency comparison PRO put on the table. PRO's two clipped turns are a modest execution cost that keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 [A2.1-A2.4] reframing CON's danger list: the pills, traffic, and medical-crash scenes need a stethoscope not a gun, and in the knife scene the fast officer is the one who produces the fatality—forcing CON for the rest of the debate to defend the marginal minutes with a hypothetical third-party attack rather than the scenes it opened with.</best_rebuttal>
